content: Enuresis, commonly referred to as bedwetting, affects approximately 20% of five-year-old children and persists into adulthood in about 2% of cases. While spontaneous remission is common, the condition can have significant social, emotional, and psychological consequences. Tricyclic antidepressants have been utilized as a treatment for enuresis since the 1960s. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of tricyclic and related drugs in comparison to other interventions for treating enuresis in children. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials that compared tricyclics or related drugs to other treatments, including combination therapies involving tricyclics. Trials focused on daytime wetting were excluded. A total of 64 trials involving 4,071 children met the inclusion criteria. The quality of many of these trials was suboptimal, with some comparisons being addressed by single studies. Minor adverse effects, such as dizziness, headache, mood changes, gastrointestinal discomfort, and neutropenia, were frequently reported in 30 trials. Serious adverse effects were possible but not reported in the included studies. Seven trials reported no adverse effects. Tricyclics were found to be more effective than placebo, particularly for short-term outcomes. For example, imipramine reduced the number of wet nights by approximately one per week compared to placebo (mean difference [MD] -0.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] -1.40 to -0.50; 4 trials, 347 children). Additionally, fewer children on imipramine failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights compared to placebo (78% versus 95%, relative risk [RR] 0.74, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.90; 12 trials, 831 children). Amitriptyline and desipramine were also more effective than placebo, while nortriptyline and mianserin showed no significant difference. However, the effects of tricyclics were not sustained after treatment cessation, with relapse rates of 96% for imipramine compared to 97% for placebo. Combination therapy with imipramine and oxybutynin was more effective than placebo. At the end of treatment, 33% of children in the combination group failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights compared to 78% in the placebo group (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.78; 1 trial, 47 children). At follow-up, 45% of children in the combination group were wetting compared to 79% in the placebo group (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.99; 1 trial, 36 children). There was insufficient evidence to determine the effects of different doses of tricyclics or to compare the efficacy of different tricyclic drugs. When compared to desmopressin, treatment outcomes were similar. However, when imipramine was compared to a combination of desmopressin and oxybutynin, the combination therapy was more effective. For instance, the combination resulted in one fewer wet night per week (MD 1.07, 95% CI 0.06 to 2.08) and a lower proportion of children failing to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights (36% versus 87% for imipramine alone, RR 2.39, 95% CI 1.35 to 4.25; 1 trial, 45 children). Tricyclics were less effective than alarm therapy. Although there was no significant difference in the number of wet nights, 67% of children on imipramine failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights compared to only 17% of children using alarms (RR 4.00, 95% CI 1.06 to 15.08; 1 trial, 24 children). Alarm therapy also demonstrated a more sustained effect after treatment cessation, with 100% of children on imipramine relapsing compared to 58% of children using alarms (RR 1.67, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.69; 1 trial, 24 children). Imipramine was more effective than simple behavioral therapies, such as star charts combined with placebo, during treatment. For example, imipramine reduced the number of wet nights by approximately one per week (MD -0.80, 95% CI -1.33 to -0.27; 1 trial, 250 children). However, imipramine was less effective than complex behavioral therapies, such as a three-step program or a combination of motivational therapy and computer-led education. For instance, 61% of children on imipramine failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights compared to 33% on the three-step program (RR 1.83, 95% CI 1.08 to 3.12; 1 trial, 72 children). Tricyclics were more effective than restricted diets, with 99% of children on restricted diets failing to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights compared to 84% on imipramine (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.93; 1 trial, 147 children). However, there was insufficient evidence to evaluate the effects of tricyclics compared to other miscellaneous interventions. Combination therapy with imipramine and oxybutynin was more effective than imipramine monotherapy. At the end of treatment, children in the combination group experienced approximately two fewer wet nights per week (MD -2.10, 95% CI -2.99 to -1.21; 1 trial, 63 children). Additionally, 48% of children in the combination group failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights compared to 74% in the monotherapy group (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.92; 2 trials, 101 children). At follow-up, 45% of children in the combination group were wetting compared to 83% in the monotherapy group (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.92; 1 trial, 36 children). When imipramine combined with desmopressin was compared to imipramine monotherapy, no significant differences in outcomes were observed. However, when imipramine plus desmopressin was compared to desmopressin monotherapy, the combination therapy was more effective. For example, 15% of children in the combination group failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights compared to 40% in the desmopressin monotherapy group (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.83; 1 trial, 86 children). Tricyclics combined with alarm therapy were not more effective than alarm monotherapy, alarm combined with desmopressin, or alarm combined with nortriptyline. Similarly, the addition of a tricyclic to other behavioral therapies did not significantly alter treatment outcomes. In conclusion, tricyclics were effective in reducing the number of wet nights during treatment but did not provide sustained benefits after treatment cessation, with most children relapsing. In contrast, alarm therapy demonstrated superior shortand long-term outcomes. There was some evidence suggesting that combining tricyclics with anticholinergics may enhance efficacy compared to tricyclic monotherapy.
